Well, it's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day when my husband and I were supposed to go to our usual Saturday morning farmers market. We’ve gone every Saturday for, gosh, it has to be five or six years now. We have our favorite vendor who sells those wonderful heirloom tomatoes, and we usually get a coffee from the little cart near the entrance... it's a whole routine, you know? I just look at it sitting on my nightstand and think about how much effort it takes to focus on the words, and I just turn on the TV instead, even though I'm not really watching it. 

Even with the kids... I mean, I still love my third graders, I really do. They have such funny little personalities. Just last week, little Tommy tried to convince me that his dog actually ate his math worksheet, which is such a cliché, but he was so earnest about it. Normally, I would have found that so endearing and had a good chuckle about it with the other teachers in the breakroom. But this time, I just felt... flat. I just gave him another copy and moved on. It just feels like the color has been drained out of everything, you know? Like I'm just going through the motions, but the joy I usually get from these things is just... missing. It's really unsettling, to be honest. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, but it just hasn't happened.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no, not most of the day, and certainly not nearly every day. I mean, "depressed" or "hopeless" are such strong words, aren't they? It sounds so... final. And that's just not how I feel at all. 

I'll admit, I've had my moments of feeling overwhelmed, or maybe a bit tearful. Like last Tuesday, I think it was. Yes, Tuesday, because it was right after our grade-level planning meeting where the principal dropped yet another set of assessment rubrics on us for this new curriculum. I remember walking out to my car in the parking lot—I always park under this big oak tree near the playground to keep the sun off my seats—and I just sat behind the steering wheel for a good ten minutes, staring at the windshield, feeling this wave of... I don't know, frustration? A little bit of sadness that teaching just isn't as joyful as it used to be. I might have even let out a sigh or two, just feeling the weight of all those expectations. 

But then I turned the key in the ignition, the radio came on—it was a lovely jazz piece, actually—and I drove home. By the time I pulled into my driveway and saw my husband out front, pruning the azalea bushes by the porch, that heavy feeling had mostly lifted. We went inside, I chopped the vegetables for a stir-fry, and we had a perfectly pleasant evening talking about his day at the hardware store. 

So, you see, it’s not this dark cloud following me around from morning until night. I’m not waking up in despair or going to bed feeling like there’s no point to anything. The mornings are actually quite nice, as I mentioned, with my tea and getting ready for the day. And once I’m in the classroom with the children, my mind is completely occupied with them. You can't be hopeless when a third-grader is excitedly showing you a picture they drew of a dinosaur with a jetpack! It’s just not possible. 

It's really only when I'm faced with the administrative side of things, all the changes and the red tape that they keep piling on us this year, that I feel a bit down or stressed. But it passes. It doesn't consume my whole day, and it certainly isn't an everyday occurrence. Most days, I'm just going about my routine, getting things done, and feeling perfectly fine, if a little annoyed by the school board's decisions. But hopeless? Depressed all day? No, definitely not.

Oh, goodness, no. My appetite is exactly the same as it always is, and my weight hasn't budged a single pound. I'm very regimented about my meals, you see. I really have to be, with my teaching schedule.

Oh, goodness, no. Moving slowly? If I moved slowly, those third graders would have the entire classroom dismantled by morning recess! You really have to be quick on your feet in this profession. I’ve always been a rather brisk walker anyway—my husband always jokes that I march instead of walk, especially when we're at the grocery store or trying to get to our seats at the community theater. 

And my speaking pace hasn't changed a bit, either. When you teach eight- and nine-year-olds, you have to speak very clearly and at a very deliberate, normal pace. If you talk too slowly, you completely lose their attention and they start poking each other with erasers, and if you talk too fast, they miss the instructions entirely and you just have to repeat yourself anyway. So I’m definitely talking at my usual, steady speed. 

And as for being restless or fidgety... no, I wouldn't say that at all. I can sit perfectly still when the situation calls for it. For example, every day after lunch, we have D.E.A.R. time—that stands for Drop Everything And Read, I'm not sure if they still call it that in other districts, but we do—and it is twenty minutes of absolute quiet. I sit right at my desk at the front of the room to model good reading behavior for them. You really have to show them how to sit quietly with a chapter book, because they are just like little mirrors, you know? They mimic absolutely everything you do. If I were sitting up there bouncing my leg or tapping my fingernails on the desk, within five minutes, you'd have twenty-two children tapping and bouncing along with me, and it would be utter chaos. 

Plus, in the evenings, I sit in my favorite floral armchair in the living room—it’s a lovely Ethan Allen piece we found at an estate sale years ago, incredibly supportive for the lower back—and I grade papers for a solid hour or two without needing to jump up and pace around. I just sit there with my red pen, completely focused on their worksheets while my husband watches his history documentaries. If I were fidgety, I'd probably be making stray marks all over their spelling tests! So, no, I’m not sluggish and I’m certainly not jittery. My pace, physically and verbally, is exactly the same as it’s always been.

Oh, no, definitely not. In fact, I think my concentration is as sharp as it’s ever been, mostly out of pure necessity! 

You know, I read an article in an education journal a few years back that claimed teachers make more minute-by-minute decisions than brain surgeons. And honestly, I completely believe it. You simply cannot survive in a third-grade classroom if you can't think clearly or make a firm decision on the spot. Just this morning, for instance, during our math block—we’re working on fractions right now, which is always a notoriously tricky concept for eight-year-olds to grasp—I had to monitor three different small groups, remember exactly which students needed the modified worksheets because of their accommodations, and decide right then and there how to re-explain numerators to a child who was just staring completely blankly at me. And I had to do all of that while simultaneously making sure nobody at the back table was building towers out of the plastic math manipulatives instead of counting them. You just can't manage that kind of multitasking if you're in a fog.

And as for concentrating, well, when I sit down with my grading in the evening, I am laser-focused. I have to be. When you're reading twenty-two short paragraphs on the water cycle, you really have to pay close attention to catch the simple spelling errors versus the actual conceptual misunderstandings. If a student writes "condensation" instead of "precipitation," I need to spot that immediately so I can pull them aside the next day during independent work time to correct it. I couldn't possibly do my job effectively if my mind was wandering or if I couldn't make a decision about how to grade a rubric. 

So, no, no trouble thinking clearly at all. My mind is perfectly sharp. It might be filled to the absolute brim with state curriculum standards, permission slips, and PTA newsletter deadlines, but it is definitely clear!

I might have even let out a sigh or two, just feeling the weight of all those expectations. \n\nBut then I turned the key in the ignition, the radio came on—it was a lovely jazz piece, actually—and I drove home. By the time I pulled into my driveway and saw my husband out front, pruning the azalea bushes by the porch, that heavy feeling had mostly lifted. We went inside, I chopped the vegetables for a stir-fry, and we had a perfectly pleasant evening talking about his day at the hardware store. \n\nSo, you see, it’s not this dark cloud following me around from morning until night. I’m not waking up in despair or going to bed feeling like there’s no point to anything. The mornings are actually quite nice, as I mentioned, with my tea and getting ready for the day. And once I’m in the classroom with the children, my mind is completely occupied with them. You can't be hopeless when a third-grader is excitedly showing you a picture they drew of a dinosaur with a jetpack! It’s just not possible. \n\nIt's really only when I'm faced with the administrative side of things, all the changes and the red tape that they keep piling on us this year, that I feel a bit down or stressed. But it passes. It doesn't consume my whole day, and it certainly isn't an everyday occurrence. Most days, I'm just going about my routine, getting things done, and feeling perfectly fine, if a little annoyed by the school board's decisions. But hopeless? Depressed all day? No, definitely not.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like eating more or less than usual or losing or gaining weight without trying?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, no. My appetite is exactly the same as it always is, and my weight hasn't budged a single pound. I'm very regimented about my meals, you see. I usually toss in a handful of blueberries if they're in season at the farmer's market, or maybe a few chopped walnuts, and I eat every last bite while I drink my tea before I head out the door. \n\nAnd then for lunch, I always pack my own. The cafeteria food at school... well, let's just say it leaves a lot to be desired, and I simply cannot stomach another slice of that dreadful square pizza they serve on Fridays. So I bring a turkey sandwich on whole wheat, a little Tupperware container of carrot sticks, and usually a Honeycrisp apple. I sit in the teachers' lounge, usually trying to grade a few spelling tests or just trying to get five minutes of quiet away from the kids, and I eat the whole thing. I haven't been skipping meals or leaving half my sandwich behind, nothing like that. I just wouldn't make it through the afternoon slump if I didn't eat my lunch. \n\nDinner is just as normal, too. Like I mentioned, my husband and I are very routine-oriented. We do our weekly grocery shopping on Saturday mornings at the Kroger down the street—we like to go right at 7:30 AM before the aisles get all clogged up with carts—and we plan out all our meals for the week on this little magnetic whiteboard on the fridge. We stick to the list, and we eat what we planned. I haven't been snacking more, either. I know some people eat when they're stressed, and heaven knows this new curriculum rollout is enough to make anyone want to dive into a pint of ice cream, but I'm just not an emotional eater. \n\nAs for my weight, it's been exactly the same for... oh, it must be ten years now. I know this for a fact because I have this one pair of navy slacks, they're from Talbots, and I wear them to all the parent-teacher conferences because they look so professional but they're still comfortable enough to sit in those tiny chairs. I step on the scale in our master bathroom every Sunday morning before my shower, just out of habit really, and it always says the exact same number, give or take a pound for water weight. I just sit there with my red pen, completely focused on their worksheets while my husband watches his history documentaries. Well, no, not really. I mean, my thinking is perfectly clear. I have to be clear-headed, don't I? When you're managing a classroom of twenty-two eight-year-olds, you simply cannot afford to have a foggy brain. You have to be sharp. You have to know exactly what's happening at all times.

I noticed that immediately, by the way! I had to redirect them, check the measurements of the first group, and pause the video for the second group to explain evaporation, all within the span of about five minutes. You can't do that if you're struggling to concentrate. 

And decision-making? Oh, I make hundreds of decisions a day. Should I let Tommy go to the bathroom now or make him wait until after the spelling test? Is Sarah's stomachache real or is she just trying to get out of reading out loud? Do I have time to run to the office and check my mailbox before the bell rings? I make these decisions in a split second, constantly. 

Now, am I distracted sometimes? Yes, absolutely. But I'm distracted by the sheer volume of things I'm expected to keep track of. When I'm trying to grade papers at home and my mind wanders, it's not because I can't concentrate, it's because I'm suddenly remembering that I need to email the parents about the upcoming field trip, or that I forgot to submit the weekly attendance report the district is now demanding by 4:00 PM on Fridays instead of Monday mornings. It's the administrative overload that pulls my focus, not some sort of cognitive issue. My mind is sharp as a tack, it's just being pulled in a dozen different directions by people who have no idea what it actually takes to run a classroom! So, no, I wouldn't say I'm struggling to think clearly or make decisions. I'm just overwhelmed by the sheer number of things I have to think about.
